papers.title: Sleep characteristics and sarcopenia in patients undergoing peritoneal dialysis: nonlinear associations and a potential adiposity-related pathway.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances are common in patients undergoing peritoneal dialysis (PD), yet the pathways linking sleep characteristics to sarcopenia remain poorly understood. We examined associations of sleep duration and quality with sarcopenia and whether these associations included an indirect component involving percent body fat (PBF), with albumin and neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) as potential modifiers. This cross-sectional study included 562 patients receiving PD. Sleep was assessed by the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI). Sarcopenia was defined by 2025 Asian Working Group criteria; PBF was assessed by bioelectrical impedance. Restricted cubic splines, mediation/moderated mediation analyses, and sensitivity tests (E-values) were used. Sleep duration showed a U-shaped association with sarcopenia (p-nonlinear < 0.001), with the lowest estimated odds at approximately 7.29 h/night. PSQI score was positively associated with sarcopenia (OR = 1.12 per one-point increase). An indirect association involving PBF was observed for PSQI (ACME = 0.002, p = 0.031) and short sleep (ACME = 0.026, p = 0.030), but not for long sleep. Albumin interacted with PBF in the sarcopenia model for the PSQI (p = 0.042) and short-sleep (p = 0.031) pathways, but the indices of moderated mediation were not statistically significant. NLR showed no evidence of interaction. Mediation sensitivity analysis suggested that the observed indirect associations were not readily explained by modest residual confounding. Sleep duration and quality are associated with sarcopenia in PD patients. An indirect association involving PBF was observed for poorer sleep quality and short sleep, but not for long sleep. Albumin interacts with PBF, yet does not significantly modify the overall indirect pathway. Due to the cross-sectional design, findings are hypothesis-generating and not causal.

papers.title: Changes and trajectories in sleep duration and risk of premature all-cause and cardiovascular disease mortality.
papers.abstract: BackgroundWhile substantial evidence indicates an association between sleep and a range of chronic conditions, the potential impact of longitudinal changes in sleep on the risk of premature mortality remains poorly characterized.MethodsWe conducted a population-based cohort study using data from The Rural Chinese Cohort Study. Baseline assessments were performed during 2007-2008, with two subsequent follow-up surveys conducted in 2013-2014 and 2018-2020. A total of 13621 adults aged ⩾18 years were included after excluding participants with missing sleep duration data at baseline or the first follow-up or aged ⩾70 years at baseline. Cox proportional hazards regression models were employed to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for the associations of relative changes and trajectories of sleep duration with premature all-cause and cardiovascular disease (CVD) mortality.ResultsDuring a median follow-up of 5.07 years, the relative change in sleep duration was significantly associated with the risks of premature all-cause and CVD mortality. Compared with participants with stable sleep duration (-15% to 15%), those with a ⩾30% increase in sleep duration had a higher risk of premature all-cause (HR 1.78, 95% CI 1.28-2.47) and CVD mortality (HR 2.20, 95% CI 1.42-3.41). Sleep trajectory analyses suggested that transitions toward long sleep duration (>9 h/day) were associated with an increased risk of premature CVD mortality.ConclusionsMaintaining a stable healthy sleep duration might be important for reducing the risk of premature all-cause and CVD mortality. These findings highlight the potential value of monitoring dynamic changes in sleep duration as a modifiable target for health promotion.

papers.title: Enhancing the Suppression of Unwanted Memories During NREM Sleep.
papers.abstract: Memory suppression, the ability to exclude unwanted memories from awareness, plays a critical role in maintaining mental well-being. Whereas the mechanisms of memory suppression during wakefulness have been extensively studied, the effects of sleep on this process and its associated neural mechanisms remain understudied. Targeted memory reactivation, an experimental approach for investigating the relationship between sleep and memory processing, provides a unique opportunity to further explore this relationship. Here, we combined the Think/No-Think paradigm with targeted memory reactivation to investigate whether and how reactivating suppression processes during sleep engages its associated neural mechanisms and influences later memory performance. Participants first learned cue-associate word pairs. They were then presented with trials, each exposing a cue word, preceded by an auditory instruction requiring the participant to either retrieve or suppress the corresponding target word. Subsequently, during NREM sleep, we unobtrusively re-presented the auditory tone signaling the instruction to suppress retrieval. We found that cueing people to suppress in this manner significantly enhanced suppression-induced forgetting on a later post-sleep test, compared to pairs that were not cued during sleep. Electroencephalogram analyses revealed that reactivation of suppression instructions increased theta power and reduced the coupling strength between spindles and the slow oscillation (SO) up-states. Importantly, only reduced SO up-state-spindle coupling predicted poorer later memory retrieval for suppressed pairs. The present results suggest that the disruption of neural synchrony between SO up-state and spindles during sleep plays a critical role in enhancing subsequent suppression-induced forgetting.

papers.title: Heterogeneous perceived stress profiles and static-dynamic symptom networks of PTSD, anxiety, depression, and insomnia in firefighters: An integrated latent profile and network analysis.
papers.abstract: Firefighters are routinely exposed to occupational stress and potentially traumatic events, yet heterogeneity in perceived stress and its associations with psychopathological symptom patterns remain insufficiently understood. This study aimed to identify perceived stress profiles in Chinese firefighters and examine profile-specific cross-sectional and longitudinal associations among psychopathological symptoms. A total of 8428 Chinese firefighters were recruited, and two assessments were conducted nine months apart. Latent profile analysis was used to identify perceived stress profiles. Regularized partial correlation networks and cross-lagged panel networks were then estimated within each profile to examine cross-sectional and prospective associations among post-traumatic stress disorder, anxiety, depression, and insomnia symptoms. Three perceived stress profiles were identified: Task-related thinking (55.59%), Consistent stress perception (23.92%), and Imbalanced stress perception (20.49%). The Imbalanced stress perception profile reported the highest levels of perceived stress, whereas the Consistent stress perception profile exhibited the greatest psychopathological burden. Cross-sectional networks revealed distinct profile-specific symptom connectivity patterns, with sleep disturbance, arousal, and feelings of failure showing the highest expected influence, respectively. Longitudinal networks further revealed profile-specific temporal associations, with arousal, intrusion, and negative cognition/mood showing the highest out-expected influence, respectively. Low sleep satisfaction consistently showed the highest in-expected influence across profiles. Perceived stress configurations may provide complementary insights into psychopathological symptom burden beyond overall stress severity among firefighters. The profile-specific cross-sectional and longitudinal symptom associations highlight the potential value of person-centered approaches for mental health assessment and risk stratification, while their implications for targeted interventions require further prospective and interventional validation.

papers.title: Clocks In Sync: A mixed methods pilot feasibility trial of blue-light blocking therapy and time-restricted eating, alone or in combination for mania in bipolar disorder.
papers.abstract: Sleep and circadian disruptions are common in bipolar disorder (BD). Persons with lived and living experience (PWLEs) find chronotherapies to be of great interest, especially blue-blocking glasses (BBG, targeting the central biological clock) and time-restricted eating (TRE, targeting peripheral clocks). We conducted a mixed methods randomized, three group parallel pilot trial (clinicaltrials.gov: NCT06504342) to assess the feasibility of BBG and/or TRE (10: 14 of diurnal eating to nocturnal fasting informed by PWLE input) as an adjunctive treatment for inpatients with DSM-5-defined mania and a Young Mania Rating Scale (YMRS) ≥ 20. Participants were randomized 1:1:1 to TRE (BBG-/TRE+), BBG (BBG+/TRE-) or both (BBG+/TRE+). Feasibility was assessed through monitoring of adherence and qualitative semi-structured interviews with participants and staff were conducted to identify any challenges/barriers to implementation, and what supports might be needed. Change in the YMRS from blinded raters was a secondary outcome. Twenty-one eligible participants consented for the trial and 80% of participants (16/20) were mostly adherent or better with no differences in adherence across groups. Qualitative data highlights patient interest in chronotherapy interventions and staff support of integrating them in practice. There was also interest in shorter or flexible timing of the studied chronotherapies. Greater improvements were observed in the BBG+ groups compared to BBG-/TRE+ on the YMRS. Most inpatients with BD can adhere to circadian interventions requiring active participation in high acuity, inpatient settings. Our pilot study may inform future studies or clinical implementation of these and other low cost and scalable chronotherapies.

papers.title: A prospective longitudinal study of depressive symptoms in adolescents with narcolepsy: Excessive daytime sleepiness as a key correlate.
papers.abstract: Depressive symptoms are common in adolescents with narcolepsy, yet their longitudinal course remains insufficiently disclosed. We examined clinical correlates of depressive symptom severity and factors associated with improvement following treatment. We enrolled treatment-naïve patients aged 6 to <18 years with narcolepsy at West China Hospital between August 2023 and February 2026. Depressive symptoms were assessed by the Children's Depression Inventory (CDI), and reliable improvement was defined as a reliable change index < -1.96. Narcolepsy symptoms were evaluated using structured questionnaires, nocturnal polysomnography, and the multiple sleep latency test. Among 79 participants (mean age at onset: 10.7 ± 3.5 years, 62.0% male), 41 (51.9%) had clinically significant depression and exhibited an elevated burden of narcolepsy symptoms. Polysomnography parametric analysis did not differ by depression status. Longer disease duration (β = 0.581) and severe excessive daytime sleepiness (EDS; Epworth Sleepiness Scale [ESS] >16; β = 3.615) were independently associated with increased CDI scores. Among 46 participants followed for 11.0 ± 8.0 months, 20 (43.5%) achieved reliable improvement in depressive symptoms. These participants also exhibited pronounced declines in ESS and the Ullanlinna Narcolepsy Scale scores. Reduced EDS symptoms (OR 1.164) and reduced narcolepsy severity (OR 1.141) were associated with improvement in depressive symptoms. Depressive symptoms impose a substantial burden in adolescents with narcolepsy. Patient-reported EDS showed the most consistent relationship with depressive symptom severity and improvement during follow-up. Routine screening and longitudinal assessment of depressive symptoms should be incorporated into disease management in adolescents with narcolepsy.

papers.title: Cognitive disengagement syndrome and alexisomia: examining the moderating role of anxiety-depression symptoms, stress, and insomnia symptoms among a sample of Lebanese adults.
papers.abstract: The interplay between body and mind is at the heart of processing bodily states. Alexisomia refers to the lack of somatic awareness, whereas cognitive disengagement syndrome (CDS) is a cluster of symptoms that reflect mental sluggishness, daydreaming, and hypoactivity. Given that interoceptive accuracy relies on attention to internal signals, the hypoactive characteristics of CDS may attenuate interoceptive processing; therefore, individuals with higher CDS traits might show diminished awareness of bodily states. This study investigates the association between CDS and alexisomia, as well as the moderating effect of anxiety-depression symptoms, stress, and insomnia symptoms. A cross-sectional study was conducted among 877 Lebanese adults aged 18-70 years, recruited through snowball sampling. Data were collected using a Google Forms questionnaire that included the Adult Concentration Inventory, the Shitsu Taikan Sho Scale, the Stress Numerical Rating Scale, the Patient Health Questionnaire-4, and the Insomnia Severity Index. Of the participants, 64.3% were female, and 35.7% were male. The interaction models were adjusted over the following variables: marital status, education, and living situation. The CDS × anxiety-depression (B = -0.04, p = .011) and CDS × insomnia (B = -0.03, p = .002) interactions were significantly associated with alexisomia, whereas the CDS × stress interaction (B = -0.03, p = .076) was not statistically significant after applying heteroscedasticity-consistent standard errors. At low (-1 SD), mean, and high (+1 SD) levels of anxiety - depression and insomnia, higher CDS levels were significantly associated with higher levels of alexisomia. Additionally, higher levels of anxiety-depression and insomnia symptoms attenuated the positive association between CDS traits and alexisomia. Findings highlight an interplay between symptoms of cognitive disengagement and reduced somatic awareness, while emphasizing the importance of accounting for psychological distress and sleep disturbance when studying this relationship. Understanding these interactions provides a foundation for future longitudinal research to further clarify the nature and temporal relationships among these constructs.

papers.title: Autonomic and Cortical Signatures of Sleepiness After Prolonged Sleep Deprivation: Pupillary Reflex, Hippus Oscillations, and Visual Evoked Potentials.
papers.abstract: To define physiologically interpretable visual biomarkers of progressive sleepiness during 48-hour total sleep deprivation and determine whether pupillary and cortical visual measures detect changes not captured by brief behavioral or resting cardiovascular assessments. Twenty-four healthy adults completed one rested baseline assessment and eight supervised deprivation sessions across 48 hours of continuous wakefulness. The protocol included digital pupillometry during the pupillary light reflex (PLR) and Pupillary Sleepiness Test (PST), pattern-reversal and flash visual evoked potentials (VEPs), Stanford Sleepiness Scale (SSS) ratings, selected psychophysiological tasks, and resting blood pressure and heart rate measurements. PLR latency, reaction duration, and time to minimum diameter changed early, indicating slowed reflex timing. With advanced deprivation, DDil1 and DDil2 (pupil diameters at predefined early and late stages of redilation) decreased, identifying them as recovery-phase markers beyond classical PLR indices. The absolute Pupillary Unrest Index (PUI), measuring spontaneous pupillary oscillations (hippus), rose during the first deprivation night and remained elevated; the pupil-size-normalized rPUI followed slightly later, whereas mean pupil diameter was less informative. VEPs added a cortical layer: peak latencies of the pattern-reversal P100 and N135 and flash N3 and P3 components were delayed after prolonged wakefulness. SSS ratings increased progressively, while brief psychophysiological task performance and resting cardiovascular measures remained comparatively stable. Prolonged wakefulness was reflected by a temporally organized visual biomarker profile spanning phasic pupillary reflex timing, dilation-phase recovery, tonic pupillary instability, and late cortical visual-response slowing. These findings support a candidate multimodal, non-invasive framework for objective assessment of progressive sleepiness.

papers.title: Recurrent Unexplained Fever and Suspected Promazine Toxicity: Why Probable Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome Was Left Undiagnosed in a Healthcare Worker.
papers.abstract: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) is a potentially fatal adverse reaction to dopamine-antagonist medication that can resemble sepsis. A 51-year-old woman working in healthcare experienced recurrent episodes of fever, confusion and muscle rigidity, with six hospital presentations over approximately 10 months. Her prescribed medicines included promazine and amitriptyline. During an earlier severe admission, she developed hyperthermia, agitation, shock, and a creatine kinase concentration of 7272 U/L, requiring intensive care. Investigations did not identify a unifying diagnosis. During the most recent admission, review of previous records and a non-judgemental discussion elicited possible use of additional medication for sleep and neuropathic pain, although the preparation and quantity remained unclear. Six months' supply of promazine had been approved and dispensed within the preceding three months, supporting increased access without establishing the amount ingested. The clinical pattern supported a working diagnosis of probable promazine-associated NMS, with possible concomitant amitriptyline toxicity. Promazine was discontinued three days after admission. At follow-up approximately six months later, the patient remained off promazine and reported sustained symptom resolution and no further hospital attendances. This case highlights the importance of considering NMS in unexplained fever during antipsychotic treatment, conducting repeated medication reviews, and asking sensitive questions, regardless of a patient's professional healthcare background.

papers.title: Effects of a 4-week vinyasa yoga intervention on sleep and cardiovascular health in adults with insomnia symptoms: a pilot randomized controlled trial.
papers.abstract: Vinyasa yoga (VY) yields moderate-intensity physical activity that may improve sleep and cardiovascular health (CVH). However, evidence is scarce regarding the effects of VY on CVH. This study examined the effects of a 4-week VY intervention on sleep and CVH in adults with insomnia symptoms. A total of 33 insufficiently active adults (84.8 per cent female; 78.8 per cent White; 34.9 ± 10.6 y; 28.9 kg/m2) with insomnia symptoms (Insomnia Severity Index [ISI] ≥10) were randomized to a 4-week VY intervention (n = 17) or non-active control (CON; n = 16). VY participants practiced 3×/week following pre-recorded 60-minute videos and CON maintained their current lifestyle. Resting daytime blood pressure (BP), heart rate (HR), and HR variability (HRV) were obtained at baseline and post-intervention. Sleep was measured using the ISI, actigraphy, and a sleep diary. One night during sleep assessment, participants wore a chest HR monitor to assess HRV; primary HRV outcome was root mean square of successive differences. Analyses used linear mixed models and Cohen's d effect sizes. Changes in ISI, actigraphy-, and diary-assessed sleep from baseline to post-intervention did not differ between groups (each p > .06). Changes in nocturnal HRV and daytime resting BP and HRV were not significant (each p ≥ .30). Resting HR decreased for VY (72.41 ± 2.92 to 69.50 ± 2.60 bpm) and increased for CON (70.47 ± 2.54 to 72.93 ± 2.60 bpm) (p = .047). Additionally, among highly adherent participants, VY reduced ISI scores more than CON (p = .002). VY improves insomnia symptoms among those who practice regularly. It does not appear to improve nocturnal cardiovascular physiology, and shows modest benefits on daytime cardiac parasympathetic activity. Registry: ClinicalTrials.gov; Name: Yoga for Insomnia Study; URL: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05723211; Registration ID: NCT0572321; Date of Registration: January 2, 2023.

papers.title: Longitudinal multi-night home-based sleep assessment before and after metabolic bariatric surgery: protocol for the SLEEP-BAM cohort.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances are common in people with obesity and in candidates for metabolic bariatric surgery, but sleep is often evaluated mainly through obstructive sleep apnea screening or subjective questionnaires. SLEEP-BAM aims to evaluate longitudinal changes in sleep quality from before surgery to approximately 1 year after surgery using multi-night home-based wearable monitoring. The primary objective is to assess change in Garmin Sleep Score, a pragmatic device-derived composite measure of sleep quality. This single-center, prospective, within-subject cohort study will include 50 adults scheduled for primary metabolic bariatric surgery at Catharina Hospital Eindhoven, The Netherlands. Participants will complete two 5-night home measurement periods: between 3 months and 2 weeks preoperatively and approximately 1 year postoperatively. During each period, participants will wear a Garmin Index Sleep Monitor and a research-grade upper-arm wearable and will complete sleep diaries and validated questionnaires. Objective sleep, sleep timing, peripheral oxygen saturation, photoplethysmography-derived pulse rate variability features, subjective sleep, quality of life, and clinical outcomes including percentage total weight loss will be assessed. Recruitment commenced in September 2026. Data collection is ongoing, and no participant outcome data have yet been analyzed. SLEEP-BAM will characterize sleep trajectories after metabolic bariatric surgery using repeated real-world sleep assessment. The findings may clarify how objective and subjective sleep measures change after major weight loss and support future sleep-focused interventions or wearable-derived sleep algorithms in this population. papers.title: Craniofacial Load Modifies the Interaction of Obesity and Apnea Hypopnea Index Severity in Adult Males.
papers.abstract: Multiple physiological, skeletal structural, and BMI variables determine obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) severity. To better understand how craniofacial, hyoid, and obesity measures interact, data from a population-based study was re-evaluated. Lateral facial cephalometric and polysomnographic data (2% desaturation criteria for hypopnea) were reanalyzed from a population-based study and enhanced clinic population (Wisconsin Cohort Study). Cephalometric x-rays were performed awake, upright, at end expiration. Data on craniofacial structure (45 craniofacial, 10 hyoid related), age, and obesity were re-evaluated using linear and non-linear logarithmic methods. Residual variance was assessed with hierarchical cluster analysis and classified with linear discriminant analysis. 203 male patients (141 population based and 62 clinic) were included (female numbers were inadequate and were excluded from analysis). Linear analysis of all variables explained 41.3% of AHI variance with two primary contributors of BMI (28.5%) and lower facial width (12.8%). AHI at higher levels remained unexplained. Subsequent non-linear analysis identified 3 statistical groups differing in cephalometric, age, and BMI variables contributing to AHI. Clinically, the 3 groups differed in craniofacial and hyoid (1.4%, 42%, and 67%) and BMI contributions (87.6%, 40.4%, and 19.3%) and described low, intermediate, and high levels of craniofacial load. BMI effects differed by craniofacial load. For moderate or severe levels of AHI, subjects having low craniofacial load required morbid obesity, subjects with intermediate load required a combined contribution of skeletal and BMI variables, while subjects with high load did not require obesity. In adult males, multiple craniofacial cephalometric, hyoid, age, and BMI measures interact in a non-linear manner to create AHI severity. Craniofacial and hyoid variables can be described as craniofacial load. Groups with differing craniofacial load interact differently with increasing BMI. This study supports a model using craniofacial load to better understand AHI severity rather than individual traits. 4.

papers.title: Depressive status modulates hippocampal-cortical dynamics during acute nicotine use.
papers.abstract: Nicotine use disorder shows heterogeneity in treatment response, potentially reflecting differences in underlying neural circuitry, particularly in the presence of depression. We examined real-time neural dynamics during nicotine inhalation in two chronic users - one with depression and one without - using simultaneous hippocampal recordings from responsive neurostimulation (RNS) electrodes and scalp EEG. Oscillatory activity and hippocampal-cortical connectivity were analyzed in relation to mood and craving. Oscillatory activity tracked mood in the non-depressed individual but was attenuated or reversed in the depressed individual, suggesting reduced reward-related neural responsiveness. In contrast, both participants showed reduced alpha hippocampal-cortical connectivity following nicotine use, suggesting a shift from reward-seeking to reward and relief processing. These findings support a network-based framework of nicotine-driven neural dynamics and provide preliminary evidence that depressive status may modulate these processes. Although limited to two cases, this work highlights the potential for identifying neurophysiological subtypes of nicotine users and informs future efforts toward personalized treatment approaches.

papers.title: Ion Channels and Morphology Drive Widespread Resonance in Human Cortical Interneurons.
papers.abstract: Cortical neurons respond preferentially to specific network oscillation frequencies-a phenomenon driven by membrane potential resonance. While well studied in human pyramidal neurons, adult human interneuron resonance remains largely unexplored. Using Patch-seq, acute electrophysiology, organotypic cultures, and computational modeling, we investigated the mechanisms underlying resonance across human LAMP5, VIP, PV, and SST interneurons. Resonance is significantly more prevalent in human versus mouse interneurons, peaking in parvalbumin (PV) cells. Unlike human pyramidal neurons, interneuron resonance is independent of cortical depth. Instead, resonance frequency and strength strongly correlate with low input resistance, prominent membrane voltage sag, and enriched expression of HCN1, KCNJ16, and CACNA1A ion channel genes. HCN blockade abolished resonance, while enhanced HCN-mediated sag increased resonance prevalence and strength. Finally, computational models revealed that human morphological features and ion channels sharpen frequency tuning, translating into distinct suprathreshold output under noisy, in vivo-like conditions. These findings reveal fundamental species differences governing human cortical microcircuit dynamics.

papers.title: A Human iPSC-Derived Neuron and Glioma Culture Model Reveals Increased Neuronal Excitability and Loss of GABAergic Inhibition.
papers.abstract: Gliomas engage in bidirectional interactions with neural circuits, driving hyperexcitability, disruption of excitatory-inhibitory balance, and tumor-associated seizures. Human in vitro models that enable functional interrogation of tumor-induced changes in glutamatergic-GABAergic neuronal crosstalk remain limited. We established a defined human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived culture comprising of glutamatergic neurons, GABAergic neurons, and astrocytes with and without glioma cells. Network maturation and function were characterized using immunocytochemistry, multi-electrode array recordings, and whole-cell patch-clamp electrophysiology. Neuronal cultures developed mature synaptic architecture, spontaneous coordinated network activity, and suppression of neuronal firing following treatment with the GABA-A agonist muscimol, demonstrating functional GABAergic signaling. Glioma incorporation increased spike rate, increased coordinated network activity, and reversed the response to muscimol from suppression to elevation of neuronal firing, indicating disrupted GABAergic signaling. Whole-cell patch-clamp recordings demonstrated increased intrinsic excitability of glutamatergic neurons following glioma co-culture, characterized by increased action potential firing frequency and increased action potential amplitude. This human iPSC-derived glutamatergic-GABAergic neuron model recapitulates key features of tumor-induced neuronal dysfunction while enabling complementary network- and single-cell analyses. The model provides a relevant, scalable, and accessible system for mechanistic investigation of bidirectional neuron-glioma interactions and preclinical evaluation of therapies targeting tumor-induced neuronal dysfunction.

papers.title: Clinical and Upper Airway Microbial Signatures in Severe Obstructive Sleep Apnea: Association and Prediction.
Altered EEG-derived co-fluctuation structure in disorders of consciousness.
papers.abstract: EEG-derived functional connectivity (FC) enables high-temporal-resolution probing of neural mechanisms underlying disorders of consciousness (DOC). Unlike stationary conventional FC, dynamic FC (dFC) captures fast transient neural coupling. Recent fMRI studies introduced a co‑fluctuation framework to track moment‑to‑moment connectivity change, yet whether such co-fluctuation features can quantify consciousness status remains elusive. Here, we adapt this established co-fluctuation paradigm to resting-state EEG to characterize the temporal architectures of EEG-derived FC across varying conscious states. We decomposed the co-fluctuation time series into high-amplitude frames (HAF) and low-amplitude frames (LAF), comparing their dynamics between real brain data and null models. We then analyzed co-fluctuation activities across consciousness levels at both global and local spatial scales, examining spatial variability in these patterns. By integrating HAF and LAF parameters, we evaluated their diagnostic potential for distinguishing DOC states. Results revealed reduced stability of co-fluctuations with loss of consciousness, accompanied by a shift toward random system dynamics. DOC patients exhibited reduced spatial and temporal heterogeneity in co-fluctuation activities compared to healthy controls. Both high- and low-amplitude patterns provided useful metrics for detecting consciousness levels. These findings offer novel insights into the dynamic organization of brain networks in DOC, emphasizing the significance of co-fluctuation dynamics in characterizing brain states and suggesting potential biomarkers for assessing consciousness levels. The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s11571-026-10580-7.

papers.title: Cellularized, needle-deployed intracortical arrays for brain electrophysiology.
papers.abstract: Bioelectronic medicine enables direct interfacing with native cell populations but remains limited by poor long-term integration and minimal interaction with non-electroactive cells. In contrast, regenerative medicine promotes tissue integration yet lacks bidirectional functionality. Here, we present a hybrid implantation methodology combining a tissue engineered cellularized hydrogel with a neural recording array for simultaneous delivery into the brain via needle placement. This approach enables co-localized transplantation of cells and electronics while minimizing surgical footprint. Post-implantation electrophysiological recordings show functional integration with surrounding neural tissue, demonstrating the feasibility of this platform for coupled bioelectronic sensing and regenerative capabilities. The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1557/s43579-026-01033-7.

papers.title: Assessing non-invasive glymphatic MRI markers following short-term sleep loss.
papers.abstract: The glymphatic system is a sleep-active pathway involved in clearing metabolic waste from the brain. Several non-invasive MRI indices have been proposed as proxies for assessing glymphatic function in vivo . However, it remains unclear whether these indices capture glymphatic dysregulation under short-term sleep loss. Using a large ENIGMA-sleep intervention dataset (n = 429) spanning ten international sites, we examined choroid plexus volume (ChPV), perivascular space volume (PVSV), the free water index (FWI), and the DTI-ALPS index, following habitual sleep (6-8 hours in bed), sleep restriction (3-6 hours in bed), and sleep deprivation (22-40 hours wakefulness). Sleep deprivation was primarily associated with decreased PVSV and ALPS and increased FWI; sleep restriction with the inverse pattern. However, coupling between MRI indices was limited, and models assuming a shared underlying glymphatic system underperformed. Age-related alterations were dissociable from sleep-related alterations and mimicked patterns previously interpreted as glymphatic dysfunction in the literature. Moreover, PVSV increased during the day, whereas ALPS and FWI followed a divergent, anticorrelated trajectory. Our findings suggest that these MRI indices reflect distinct physiological processes; and that sleep loss may influence brain fluid dynamics primarily by modulating inflow resistance through expansion and contraction of the PVS.

papers.title: Real-time wearable detection of respiratory infections in pediatric transplant households.
papers.abstract: Consumer-grade wearables can continuously and longitudinally measure health signals such as heart rate (HR), activity, and sleep. While changes in these signals have been implicated in the early detection of infection (e.g., influenza, SARS-CoV-2) and real-time alerting systems have been developed, evidence from prospective deployment in pediatric transplant households remains limited. Here, we study the application of a resting heart rate (RHR)-based real-time alerting algorithm to detect respiratory virus infection in a cohort of solid organ transplant recipients and their household members (n=146) in a Phase IV clinical trial ( NCT06161454 ). Reliable and efficient alerting for infection events may be particularly relevant for this population, enabling isolation, clinical management, and/or treatment. Of 31 antigen-test outcomes, nearly all (29/31, 93.5%) correspond to either influenza, COVID, or other patient-reported symptoms. We describe RHR, HR, activity, and sleep/circadian rhythm features around clinical alarm events, identifying candidate features for further investigation and algorithm improvement.

papers.title: Discrete cortico-hippocampal circuit states underlie mood state transitions in depression.
papers.abstract: The hippocampus has long been implicated in depression, yet the underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Leveraging precision functional mapping in densely sampled individuals and large cross-sectional cohorts, and validating key results in direct intracranial EEG recordings from the human brain, we show that hippocampal connectivity alternates between two discrete and opposing network states on the order of minutes: one dominated by default mode network (DMN) coupling and another by sensorimotor system (SM) coupling. This dynamic switching is a fundamental property of hippocampal function in both healthy brains and in major depressive disorder (MDD). In MDD, this equilibrium is disrupted, such that the DMN-dominant state is overrepresented. In densely sampled individuals, hippocampus-DMN coupling tracks symptom fluctuations over time and normalizes after electroconvulsive therapy (ECT), which drives switches in hippocampal connectivity away from the DMN-dominant state and toward the SM-dominant state-an effect that was closely linked to a positive treatment response. Direct intracranial recordings in patients with MDD identified analogous fluctuations in hippocampal-DMN theta synchrony, which tracks symptom fluctuations over hours and days. Together, these findings identify a dynamic cortico-hippocampal mechanism underlying depression and indicate that successful neuromodulation treatments such as ECT act in part by restoring a dynamic equilibrium in hippocampal network connectivity.

papers.title: Longitudinal Pain Profiles and Their Clinical and Genetic Correlates in 624,996 U.S. Veterans.
papers.abstract: Pain varies in its intensity and course, yet much of our understanding of pain is based on cross-sectional assessments or longitudinal studies of selected clinical populations. Routinely collected electronic health record data may enable characterization of longitudinal pain patterns at scale. To identify longitudinal pain profiles among U.S. Veterans and characterize their clinical and polygenic correlates. Cohort study using electronic health record and genomic data from the Million Veteran Program, with up to 16 years of pain assessments collected between 2000 to 2025. U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs health care system. Million Veteran Program participants assigned to African-like, Admixed American-like, East Asian-like, European-like, or South Asian-like genetically inferred ancestry groups who have at least three years of outpatient numeric rating scale pain records. Outpatient pain ratings and polygenic scores for psychiatric, sleep, and substance use traits. Pain profiles were identified using Gaussian finite mixture modeling of pain intensity, directional change, and within-person variability. Profiles were characterized by pain, psychiatric and substance use diagnoses, opioid exposure, body mass index, and polygenic scores. Among 624,996 participants (Mean [SD] age at first pain rating=53.4 [13.5] years; 568,833 [91.0%] male), 51,731,567 outpatient pain ratings were analyzed. Three profiles were identified: stable no pain, stable mild pain, and mild-to-moderate increasing pain. Compared with the stable no pain profile, the increasing pain profile had higher odds of chronic pain (OR=21.14 [95% CI: 18.96-23.57]), opioid use disorder (OR=9.32 [95% CI: 8.31-10.45]), opioid exposure (OR=8.61 [95% CI: 8.41-8.83]), major depressive disorder (OR=3.77 [95% CI: 3.67-3.87]), and posttraumatic stress disorder (OR=3.72 [95% CI: 3.61-3.84]). Associations were attenuated but remained after adjustment for mean pain severity. Polygenic scores for depression, insomnia, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, and tobacco use disorder were the most consistent predictors of increasing pain across the three largest genetically inferred ancestry groups. Longitudinal modeling of routinely collected pain scores identified pain profiles associated with clinical burden and polygenic liability. These profiles captured clinically meaningful information beyond mean pain severity alone, highlighting the value of longitudinal pain phenotyping in electronic health record data. Question: Can pain scores collected in outpatient care identify clinically meaningful pain profiles among U.S. Veterans?Findings: In this cohort study of 624,996 Veterans with more than 51 million pain ratings across up to 16 years, three pain profiles were identified: stable no pain, stable mild pain, and mild-tomoderate increasing pain. Profiles differed in clinical burden even after accounting for mean pain severity and were associated with polygenic liability for psychiatric, sleep, and substance use traits.Meaning: Routinely collected pain scores can be used to characterize heterogeneity in the course of pain and factors associated with more burdensome pain patterns.

papers.title: Coupled neuro-fluid dynamics in human bioelectromagnetism.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetoencephalography (MEG) are widely interpreted as direct, non-invasive measures of neural population activity, assuming surrounding tissue and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) act as passive volume conductors that distorts but do not contribute to signal generation. Using conductive-fluid phantom experiments, structural magnetic resonance imaging, and in vivo EEG and MEG recordings, the present report challenges this assumption. Mechanically driven conductive fluid generated structured, oscillatory, source-localizable electromagnetic signals resembling M/EEG in the absence of neural tissue, and interindividual differences in CSF volume systematically moderated M/EEG signal amplitude. These findings suggest that, at the scales accessed by invasive and non-invasive electrophysiology, electromagnetic and mechanical processes form a coupled system in which contributions of neural currents and fluid motion cannot readily be uniquely separated.

papers.title: Somnus, a tunable, open-source platform for automated EEG sleep scoring in physiological and disease mouse models.
papers.abstract: Many studies using mouse models of human brain disorders rely on extended recordings of brain electrical activity through electroencephalogram, or EEG. The features that researchers measure in these recordings, such as seizures and epileptiform activity, are deeply influenced by whether the animal is awake, in non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, or in rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. Because total sleep duration varies naturally across animals, rigorous experimental comparisons require classifying the sleep state of every few seconds of a recording. Manual annotation is highly labor-intensive, often requiring hours per subject. While automated scoring tools accelerate this process, they are typically trained exclusively on healthy cohorts and frequently fail when applied to disease models that exhibit atypical or fragmented sleep architecture. Somnus is an open-source Python package designed to automate rodent sleep staging using EEG, muscle activity (EMG), and optional video-tracking data. It includes a robust base model trained on diverse recordings from six independent laboratories, enabling out-of-the-box classification across various equipment setups without requiring prior manual labeling. A central feature of Somnus is its capacity for rapid adaptation to pathological sleep structure. The software provides a graphical interface that directs researchers to the specific epochs where the base model is least certain. Users can manually correct these targeted epochs in a built-in viewer by comparing the model's classification to the raw EEG signal and video, and then use their corrections to fine-tune the model. This workflow empowers researchers to generate accurate custom scorers for complex disease models or novel treatments with just a few minutes of manual correction, bypassing the need to hand-score entire experimental cohorts or develop their own models from scratch.

papers.title: A hippocampal digital Twin reveals latent structure in freely flying bats.
papers.abstract: 1Concurrent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), large-scale neuronal recording, and behavioral tracking have enabled increasingly powerful predictive models of brain-behavior relationships. Yet predictive accuracy does not automatically yield interpretable principles of neural organization, particularly during natural behavior, where the relevant variables computed are often unknown in advance. Here, we developed a functional digital twin of the hippocampus, trained jointly on large-scale neural activity and self-directed three-dimensional flight in freely flying bats. A multi-modal, multitask transformer accurately predicted both neural activity and behavior, outperformed standard approaches, and generalized across recording sessions. Interrogating the model's representations suggested a form of hippocampal generalization across self-selected trajectories that was not apparent in physical coordinates, but was plainly visible in the model's low-dimensional latent space. We confirmed this organization directly in the recorded neural activity: neurons fired at corresponding stages of spatially distinct paths connecting the same origin and destination, preserving their relative firing order even as their firing fields shifted with the path. Analysis of neuron-specific readouts further identified functional relationships among neurons that generalized from flight to waking rest and sleep, brain states never used for training, and differed systematically between the hippocampal subregions CA1 and CA3. Together, these results show how AI-based functional digital twins can complement conventional analysis by generating testable hypotheses about neural organization during natural behavior.

papers.title: 5-HT1A Antagonist WAY-100635 Prevents Chronic Neurodegeneration and Immune Activation After TBI.
papers.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) initiates secondary neurodegeneration that compromises interconnected neural circuits and contributes to persistent visual and neurobehavioral impairment. Pharmacological strategies that preserve vulnerable neurons and synapses while limiting chronic neuroinflammation remain an unmet therapeutic need. We previously identified the serotonin 1A receptor (5-HT1A) antagonist WAY-100635 through screening human stem cell-derived retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) and demonstrated that it promotes neuroprotection through cyclic adenosine monophosphate-dependent mitochondrial biogenesis. Here, we investigated whether post-injury treatment extends this neuroprotective efficacy to cerebral and visual circuitry following TBI. Male C57BL/6J mice aged 2-3 months underwent unilateral controlled cortical impact (CCI) involving the left visual cortex. Mice were randomly assigned to sham, untreated injury or treated injury groups, with 3-10 sham controls and 5-8 mice per injury group across experiments. WAY-100635 was administered intraperitoneally at 5 mg/kg daily, beginning 1 hour after injury and continuing for 6 weeks. Therapeutic efficacy was assessed using motor and psychological-health-relevant risk-taking/behavioral disinhibition by elevated-plus-maze assessment, visual electrophysiology, optokinetic responses, diffusion magnetic resonance imaging, and retinal and cortical histopathology. Unilateral cortical injury produced bilateral RGC dysfunction and loss, with greater degeneration in the eye contralateral to the injured hemisphere, consistent with predominantly crossed murine visual projections. WAY-100635 significantly preserved RGC survival and function, improved visual acuity and contrast sensitivity, and preserved visually evoked cortical responses to contralateral eye stimulation. Diffusion MRI revealed bilateral visual pathway abnormalities, with treatment selectively normalizing fractional anisotropy and radial kurtosis in the optic tract ipsilateral to cortical injury. In perilesional cortex, treatment preserved neuronal cell bodies and synapses detected by synaptophysin immunoreactivity while markedly reducing microglial/macrophage activation and reactive astrogliosis. These effects were accompanied by improved early motor performance and attenuation of injury-associated increases in open-arm exploration in the elevated plus maze. Cortical cavity volume was not significantly reduced, supporting preferential protection of vulnerable circuitry surrounding and connected to the primary lesion. These findings identify post-injury WAY-100635 treatment as a novel therapeutic intervention that combines neuronal and synaptic preservation with reduced chronic glial activation and improved functional outcomes. They support further translational development of serotonin 1A receptor antagonism to limit secondary neurodegeneration and the visual and neurobehavioral consequences of TBI.

papers.title: Excitation-contraction coupling plasticity is revealed upon RyR2 depletion in adult mouse ventricular myocytes.
papers.abstract: Ryanodine receptor 2 (RyR2) is central to cardiac excitation-contraction coupling (ECC), translating electrical signals into sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) Ca 2+ release and mechanical contraction. Although constitutive deletion of RyR2 is lethal, adult hearts can withstand a significant reduction in RyR2 expression without overt ECC dysfunction. We hypothesized that ECC possesses intrinsic homeostatic plasticity that rapidly adapts to acute RyR2 loss to maintain cardiac performance. Using an adult tamoxifen-inducible RyR2 conditional knockout (RyR2cKO) mouse model, we evaluated cardiac structure, electrophysiology, and intracellular Ca 2+ dynamics. RyR2cKO mice survived for weeks with <10% residual RyR2 protein expression. In vivo echocardiography and electrocardiography revealed normal cardiac structure and function. Confocal Ca 2+ imaging in intact hearts and isolated ventricular myocytes showed preserved Ca 2+ transient (CaT) amplitude but slower release kinetics and elevated SR load. Simultaneous patch-clamp and confocal Ca 2+ imaging established that L-type Ca 2+ current ( I Ca ) and ECC gain were maintained in RyR2cKO myocytes. Expression of Ca V 1.2, NCX, and phospholamban remained unchanged, whereas SERCA2a, IP 3 receptor, and VMP1 levels decreased. Pharmacological inhibition of IP 3 receptors did not suppress CaT, ruling out alternative SR channel compensation. These findings reveal remarkable intrinsic ECC plasticity, where high RyR2 channel reserve, elevated SR Ca 2+ load, and CaT autoregulation collectively maintain cardiac Ca 2+ cycling and contractile function despite profound RyR2 depletion. Deletion of RyR2, a critical channel for cardiac excitation-contraction coupling (ECC), is embryonically lethal; however, adult cardiomyocytes can tolerate a significant reduction in RyR2 expression without overt dysfunction. We show that mouse hearts and cardiomyocytes with a 90% reduction in RyR2 expression show preserved Ca 2+ handling. Compensation for reduced RyR2 levels does not involve overt remodeling of the ECC machinery or cardiac structure.Cardiomyocytes have a RyR2 reserve and employ autoregulation to maintain ECC fidelity, uncovering homeostatic plasticity as a regulatory mechanism of ECC.Reduced RyR2 expression is often observed in heart disease; however, it may not contribute to the pathology.

papers.title: Spontaneous Hemodynamic Oscillations during Sleep Coordinate Directional CSF Flow in the Subarachnoid Space and Ventricles.
papers.abstract: During sleep, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) flow is enhanced and thought to facilitate clearance of metabolic waste from the brain. Human imaging has shown that sleep is associated with large waves of bulk CSF flow in the fourth ventricle; however, the CSF flow dynamics around brain tissue are unknown. Here, we investigated how CSF flow is organized across the subarachnoid space, a key site both for fluid exchange across cortical surface and for transport out of the cranium. We used an MRI technology at 7 Tesla that simultaneously measures cortical hemodynamics and slow subarachnoid CSF flow and applied this during sleep. We found that spontaneous infraslow hemodynamic oscillations were coupled to spatially structured, directional CSF flow throughout both ventricular and subarachnoid compartments. Hemodynamic oscillations and fourth-ventricle bulk flow were both associated with brain-wide CSF flow at different phases, indicating that they reflect a single coordinated CSF movement cycle. Compared to cardiac pulsations, a canonical driver of CSF movement, hemodynamic-driven CSF flow showed a distinct directional pattern and was smaller in instantaneous amplitude but produced substantially greater cumulative displacement and thus greater potential for transport within an oscillation period. Together, these findings show that hemodynamic oscillations during sleep are coupled to temporally coordinated and directional CSF flow throughout the ventricles and subarachnoid space, suggesting that sleep-dependent neuronal activity drives fluid movement across the human brain in a distinct spatial pattern.

papers.title: A Benchmark of Unsupervised Circadian Phase Inference Methods for Bulk Transcriptomic Data.
papers.abstract: Circadian phase can be inferred from gene expression when sample collection times are unavailable, but the available methods have not been systematically compared. We compared ten unsupervised phase inference methods and two clock-gene baselines on 25 datasets with reference times (16 real datasets from five studies and 9 simulations). The primary measure was the aligned circular mean absolute error (MAE), with a permutation test for significance, circular correlations and gene-level reconstruction of rhythmicity, acrophase and amplitude were secondary outcomes. CHIRAL had the lowest mean MAE (1.80 h, 95% confidence interval 1.21-2.97 h from resampling study families). The two clock-gene baselines (2.15 and 2.20 h) were next, followed by TEMPO, CYCLOPS and CYCLOPS 2.0 (2.49-2.80 h), and the confidence intervals of these six overlapped substantially. The other six methods had mean errors of 3.91-4.86 h, compared with 5.08-5.23 h for permuted phases. Accuracy depended on the dataset and on the strength of clock-gene rhythms, and, for several methods, on the random seed and the adjustment for batch or covariates. When the inferred phases were used to analyse gene rhythms in 22 datasets, the four leading methods identified rhythmic genes with a median ROC AUC of 0.64-0.70 and recovered gene acrophases with a median error of 0.18-0.64 h. In two mouse datasets without collection times, agreement with external reference acrophases differed between methods and tissues.

papers.title: Circadian phase alignment promotes survival under predictive oxidative stress.
papers.abstract: Circadian clocks are endogenous time-keeping mechanisms that continue to oscillate with a period that approximates 24 h in the absence of cyclic environmental cues. This free-running period (FRP) varies from species to species and can vary within species across latitudinal clines. Because natural environments provide daily cues that reset circadian clocks to exactly 24 h, the importance of the FRP length is unclear. Using the cyanobacterium Synechococcus elongatus we show that the FRP length alters the alignment of a biological process with an environmental reference, known as phase angle of entrainment, across seasonal photoperiods, thereby repositioning stress-response programs relative to the external environment. This phase relationship affects the overall fitness of the organism: strains that position stress-response programs to peak at the time at which the stressor peaks outcompete their early- or late-peaking counterparts. Our results suggest that the FRP length is selected for its ability to adjust the phase angle of entrainment across seasonal photoperiods: the wild-type FRP length was uniquely plastic in its ability to adjust stress-response programs to coincide with the stressor in all photoperiod conditions. Circadian clocks are nearly universal biological timing systems that allow organisms to anticipate daily environmental changes, optimize environmental resources, and avoid environmental threats. We investigated which features of clock function promote survival fitness and which environmental conditions provide selection. A long-standing hypothesis is that the phase relationship between the internal timing mechanism and the external environment is critical for the circadian clock to confer a fitness advantage. However, because this phase relationship is influenced by the circadian period, tests of this hypothesis confound the two features. We experimentally decoupled the free-running period and the environmental phase relationship to show that the phase relationship, rather than the free-running period, confers fitness under environmental conditions that impose a selection.

papers.title: A KaiA Conformational Switch Links Day-Night Transitions to Clock Robustness.
papers.abstract: Biological clocks require mechanisms that enable transition between temporal phases and buffer against environmental fluctuations. In the cyanobacterial KaiABC-based circadian oscillator, KaiA has been regarded as a daytime activator that is passively sequestered at night. Here we define KaiA as a conformationally regulated activator and an active catalyst of the night-to-dawn transition. We identify a single linker helix, α5, that acts as a structural switch, mediating a domain-driven "tug-of-war" that sets the open-closed equilibrium in KaiA. Structure-guided mutations that shift this balance in either direction abolish stable rhythmicity both in vitro and in cells. Also, we show that substoichiometric KaiA dismantles nighttime KaiB-KaiC complexes through interactions with the KaiC C-terminal tails and likely initiates an autocatalytic feedback loop that resets the phosphorylation cycle at dawn. Furthermore, we present two independent kinetic models that offer distinct, deterministic explanations for the clock's low-temperature amplitude decline and failure at 20 °C.

papers.title: Probing the neural geometry of conscious object perception in time.
papers.abstract: Conscious object recognition is a critical brain function, key to making sense of the plethora of visual inputs and guiding adaptive behavior. Yet, the sequence of neural processing underlying conscious object recognition remains unclear. Existing proposals alternatively suggest that conscious object recognition proceeds in a "coarse-to-fine" sequence or a "fine-to-coarse" sequence. Here, we recorded high-density EEG while participants of both sexes performed a threshold-level object recognition task under different viewing conditions. Both superordinate and basic-level category information emerged early in neural activity, followed by a late superordinate category representation in an abstract format that is disentangled from low-level object features. Strikingly, in the early period, while basic-level category information positively correlated with perceptual awareness, superordinate category information negatively predicted perceptual awareness. By contrast, both superordinate and basic-level category information positively correlated with objective categorization accuracy in the early period. In the late period, both levels of category information positively correlated with awareness. These results suggest that neural processing underlying conscious object perception proceeds from the basic to the superordinate category level. Despite significant interests, the sequence of neural processing underlying conscious perception remains unclear. Here, we investigated the unfolding of neural events in time that support perceptual awareness of visual objects. Using a threshold-level object perception task involving three image conditions (normal, low-pass filtered, masked) and high-density EEG, we reveal that basic and superordinate category information both emerge early in the neural activity (at ∼100 ms), but only the basic-level category representation positively contributes to awareness. By contrast, the early superordinate category representation negatively correlates with perceptual awareness. At ∼300 ms, an abstract superordinate category representation emerges, which also positively correlates with perceptual awareness. Therefore, category-level neural processing underlying conscious object perception proceeds from the basic to the superordinate level.

papers.title: Aging Is Associated with Reduced Topographic Differentiation Between Speaking and Silent Reading.
papers.abstract: Aging affects how neural activity is organized and specialized, but its impact on neural differentiation across language tasks remains unclear. In this study, we investigated whether aging influences neural differentiation during speaking and silent reading. Fifteen young adults and 15 older adults completed speaking and silent-reading tasks in a delayed-response paradigm while we collected electroencephalography (EEG) data. We examined EEG signal strength using time-resolved global field power (GFP), spatial configuration using topographic analysis of variance (TANOVA), and task-specific neural differentiation using the global dissimilarity index (DISS). We also examined the relationship between neural and behavioral measures, including digit-span scores and speech onset time. We found that speaking was associated with higher GFP than silent reading in the 388-800 ms interval, with no significant effects of group or group × task interaction, indicating similar EEG strength across groups. TANOVA revealed age-related differences in scalp topography in the 229-334 ms and 377-538 ms intervals, a task effect in the 618-723 ms interval, and a group × task interaction in the 562-636 ms interval. Notably, young adults had greater DISS than older adults during the 508-629 ms and 660-800 ms intervals, reflecting more distinct neural configurations for speaking and reading. We did not find significant correlations between DISS or GFP and behavioral measures, and the two groups performed similarly on behavioral measures. Overall, aging was associated with reduced neural differentiation between speaking and silent reading, especially during later processing stages (e.g., motor command preparation), while preserving overall EEG activity and behavioral performance. These findings may suggest that aging reduces neural network specificity (as previously suggested) and alters spatial organization without necessarily impairing behavior.

papers.title: Cross-species multi-omics integration reveals lung alterations in acute kidney injury across mouse, pig, and human airway organoid models.
papers.abstract: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is frequently associated with the development of distant acute lung injury (ALI); however, its broader clinical impact and the underlying temporal molecular mechanisms remain incompletely characterized. We used aggregate deidentified Epic Cosmos data to describe all-cause mortality and hospital length of stay (LOS) in an AKI cohort (13,815,092 patients; 2016-2025) and a subgroup with subsequent lung injury (AKI-lung). Mechanistically, we integrated matched RNA-seq and proteomics from a hyper-acute pig model (4 h reperfusion), an established mouse model (24 h reperfusion), and primary lung organoids exposed to mtDAMP-conditioned media, using MOFA+, PROGENy, decoupleR/CollecTRI, and DIABLO. Candidates were validated in primary human donor lungs obtained from LifeLink, separated into Control (< 1.3 mg/dL, n = 5) and AKI (≥ 1.3 mg/dL, n = 5) groups based on the highest blood creatinine level measured in hospital. The AKI-lung subgroup had higher observed mortality than the overall AKI cohort (36.67% vs. 25.45%, p < 0.001). Mean hospital LOS was 11.3 versus 6.9 days in the reported AKI-lung and AKI alone queries, respectively (unadjusted p < 0.001). Multi-omics analyses cross-species indicated a temporal shift in proteogenomic coupling. In the hyper-acute pig model, we observed a largely post-translational response, including ciliary breakdown and metabolic changes. The established mouse model showed a coordinated transcriptional inflammatory response (r = 0.316), characterized by PI3K/Akt pathway activation and downregulation of vascular and immune regulators (Aplnr, Cd74). Human lung organoids exhibited transcriptional downregulation of tissue remodeling genes and persistent ATF6/ATF4-associated ER stress, consistent with a reparative phase under proteostatic strain. Unsupervised MOFA+ revealed conserved cross-species axes (Factors 6 and 7) linked to vascular repair and hemostasis. Upstream regulon analysis identified the endothelial integrity regulators, including FOXF1. Most importantly, targeted validation in primary human donor lungs confirmed a statistically significant, selective down-regulation of the core circadian regulator circadian locomotor output cycles kaput (CLOCK) transcript (p < 0.05). Aggregate clinical findings suggest an association between lung injury following AKI and worse outcome. Kidney-Lung crosstalk initiates as hyper-acute post-translational microvascular breakdown in swine and rapidly transitions into localized uncoupling of cell-autonomous pulmonary circadian machinery (CLOCK) in clinical human AKI, offering human-validated targets to intercept distant organ failure.

papers.title: Large-scale all-optical electrophysiology links excitability and connectivity to circuit dynamics in vivo.
papers.abstract: To understand neural computations, one would like to relate circuit dynamics to neuronal intrinsic excitability and connectivity. We developed tools for large-scale all-optical electrophysiology and applied them to approximately 300 layer 1 interneurons per mouse in vivo . Across two mice, targeted stimulation and voltage imaging identified 1,469 inhibitory and 5,752 directed electrical connections among 14,312 tested pairs. Presynaptic identity was more strongly associated with inhibitory post-synaptic potential (IPSP) amplitude, whereas postsynaptic identity was more strongly associated with IPSP decay time. Gap junctional and synaptic interactions had distinct spatiotemporal kernels, with corresponding signatures in spontaneous activity. Excitability measured under optogenetic stimulus predicted spiking responses to subthreshold voltage, depolarization rate, and spike history during spontaneous firing. Genetic subtypes also showed different behavioral-state-dependent voltage-to-spike relationships despite similar population-average subthreshold voltages. These measurements link cellular properties and pairwise interactions to spontaneous circuit dynamics, establishing an approach for functional circuit mapping in vivo . papers.title: Understanding Performance Plateaus and Representation Collapse in 3D MRI Transformers Trained to Classify Brain Disease.
papers.abstract: In medical imaging AI, we commonly assume that diagnostic classifiers will increase in accuracy if they are trained on more data, but in reality, their performance often plateaus. To understand this behavior, we ran a spectral analysis of 3D vision transformers, a common supervised deep learning model that can be trained to classify disease based on 3D brain MRI. For simpler classification methods such as linear discriminant analysis, the classifier performance AUC(N), when trained on a sample of size N, is known to depend on the encoder's eigenspectrum. Each class-discriminative direction in the latent space contributes only after the sample size N reaches a threshold N i = λ i /α i 2 - so the spectrum influences how performance scales with training data. Building on this theory, we show that supervised transformers compress almost all of their discriminative signal into one principal component (EVR@1 = 0.90-0.96): after this "representation collapse" happens, no further directions cross the threshold as training data increases, and accuracy plateaus. In principle, this plateau in performance could be due to either the encoder's learned feature space or the difficulty of the task. To distinguish these cases, we trained three types of supervised 3D transformers (ViT3D, MINiT, NIT) and, as a non-collapsing alternative, a frozen self-supervised encoder (DINO), to classify people with dementia or mild cognitive impairment (MCI) versus cognitively normal (CN) individuals from 3D brain MRI, using data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI). We froze each encoder and applied it to a new task, so that only the task difficulty varied. An "easy" task encoder (Dementia vs CN), transferred to the harder task (MCI vs CN), did not reproduce the plateau (MINiT threshold 9.2), but full retraining did (2758.5). The plateau is therefore due to the learned encoder, rather than task difficulty. Ranking the feature directions by the proportion of the disease signal they contain, we were able to identify a sign of representation collapse, i.e., a single dominant spike in the latent feature eigenspectrum. This spike was 11-26 times larger than predicted from the rest of the spectrum for the disease-trained (supervised) encoders, but was absent for DINO (0.66). To predict how transformer accuracy scales with the number of training scans, a large spike in the encoder spectrum suggests that the representation has collapsed and additional scans will not help; a small spike means that the signal is spread across many encoder latent space directions, and more training data should boost the classifier performance.

papers.title: Gut microbiome depletion aggravates glial-mediated Alzheimer's disease pathology through inflammatory, metabolic, and proteostatic dysregulation.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by chronic neuroinflammation, metabolic dysfunction, and impaired proteostasis. Emerging evidence suggests that the gut microbiome influences brain function through the gut-brain axis; however, the mechanisms by which this communication affects AD pathology remain poorly understood. In this study, we used humanized Drosophila AD models expressing human AD-related transgenes in glial cells to investigate how glial AD pathology influences the gut microbiome and how microbiome depletion affects behavior and disease progression. Our findings revealed significant alterations in the abundance of several gut microbial taxa, including Lactobacillus, Acetobacter, Enterococcus, Enterobacter, Pseudomonas, Leuconostoc, Providencia, and Gluconobacter, suggesting a potential interaction between the gut microbiome and AD progression. To further define the role of the gut microbiome in AD progression, we treated Drosophila with antibiotics to achieve substantial microbiome depletion (SMD) and evaluated the resulting behavioral, physiological, and molecular changes. Compared with conventional controls, flies with SMD exhibited enhanced inflammatory signaling and cell death, impaired autophagy, lipid dysregulation, and increased accumulation of amyloid β-42 (aβ42) and phospho-tau (pTau), with the extent of these changes varying among the different humanized AD models. These molecular alterations further exacerbated sleepcircadian disruption, altered locomotor performance, and worsened learning and memory deficits. Furthermore, we demonstrated a link between enhanced neuroinflammation and the accumulation of aβ42, pTau, and amyloid precursor protein (APP) proteins. Collectively, our findings demonstrate that gut microbiome depletion aggravates glial-mediated AD pathology through the coordinated disruption of inflammatory, metabolic, and proteostatic pathways, ultimately leading to behavioral dysfunction. These results identify the gut microbiome as a critical regulator of glial homeostasis and provide new insights into its contribution to the progression of neurodegenerative disorders.

papers.title: Mindfulness-based interventions for sleep disturbances, physical symptoms, and biological outcomes in women with cancer: a scoping review.
papers.abstract: Insomnia is prevalent among women with cancer and often co-occurs with fatigue, pain, and physiological dysregulation, yet these domains are rarely examined together in mindfulness-based intervention (MBI) research. To map the evidence on MBIs for insomnia in this population and examined how physical symptoms and biological outcomes have been assessed alongside sleep. Following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, eight databases were searched from inception to January 2026. Eligible studies included adult women with cancer receiving an MBI and reporting sleep outcomes. Data were charted on study characteristics, intervention features, sleep measures, physical symptoms, and biomarkers, and synthesized using tables and visual mapping. Thirty-nine studies were included. Most reported improvements in sleep, while fewer assessed fatigue, pain, or other physical symptoms, and only a small subset included biological markers. Concordance across sleep, physical, and biological domains was limited, with substantial heterogeneity in intervention format and dose. MBIs consistently improve sleep in women with cancer, but multidomain (sleep, physical, biological) integration remains limited due to heterogeneity. Heterogeneity in populations, interventions, comparators, and outcome measures precludes broad implementation across oncology settings. Standardized, adequately powered, mechanism-informed studies are needed to identify the most appropriate MBIs for specific patient groups and clinical contexts.

papers.title: [Analysis of erectile dysfunction and its associated factors in male patients undergoing peritoneal dialysis].
papers.abstract: Objective To investigate the prevalence proportion and influencing factors of erectile dysfunction in male patients receiving peritoneal dialysis (PD), and to provide a basis for clinical intervention. Methods A total of 170 male patients undergoing maintenance PD in Jinling Hospital from January to June 2025 were selected as the study subjects. And the international erectile function index-5 was used to evaluate sexual function of the patients. The general data, dialysis adequacy, nutritional status and other clinical indicators were collected. The logistic regression analysis was used to identify the influence factors of erectile dysfunction in the patients with PD. Results The incidence of erectile dysfunction in male patients with PD was 45.3%. And univariate analysis showed that age, education level, smoking history, dialysis-related symptoms and depressive status were significantly correlated with erectile dysfunction in male patients (all P<0.05）. Ordered logistic regression analysis identified age, sleep duration, smoking history, albumin and total cholesterol as independent risk factors for erectile dysfunction in male patients with PD. Conclusion The incidence of erectile dysfunction is relatively high in male patients with PD which is influenced by various physiological and psychological factors. Clinically, attention should be paid to patients' nutritional status, sleep quality, and other factors, with comprehensive interventions implemented to improve sexual function and overall quality of life.
